Follow these writing rules. They matter as much as the content:

- Bold used as body emphasis throughout -- reserve bold for a rare callout
- A short rhetorical question with a canned answer -- collapse into one direct statement
- Short buildup, then a reveal: "The best part: it learns." -- state it as a plain sentence
- Emoji or decorative checkmarks in body text -- cut them
- An em dash, section sign or middle dot written as an HTML entity -- write the plain character
- Throat-clearing openers: "needless to say", "at the end of the day" -- state the point directly from the first sentence
- Fake ID tags opening list items: "R-1.", "US-01" -- number the list plainly
- Marketing adjectives: seamless, robust, cutting-edge -- say what is actually true
- The "not just X but Y" construction -- make the point once
- Body paragraphs nearly identical in length -- vary them with what each paragraph has to do
- A significance clause bolted to a sentence: ", underscoring the..." -- delete it, or make it a claim with something behind it
- Three parallel -ing items in a series -- keep the one that carries information
- Fake-humility feedback requests: "would love your feedback on this" -- cut them
- Horizontal rules dropped between sections -- headings already separate sections
- Headings Capitalised Like This -- sentence case
- Vague intensifiers with no number behind them: very, really, quite, significantly -- say how much, or cut the word
- Unnamed authority: "studies show", "experts agree" -- name the actual source, or cut the claim

Now write the following. Return only the requested text.
Write a job posting for a senior backend engineer at a mid-sized fintech company. Around 250 words.

## Senior backend engineer

Meridian Pay, Chicago or remote (US time zones). $185k–$215k, equity, full benefits.

We move money for about 4,000 small businesses — payroll runs, vendor payments, and the reconciliation work that sits underneath both. Roughly $9B settled last year across a platform that started as a Rails monolith in 2019 and is now a mix of that monolith and eleven Go services. You would own two of them.

The work is less glamorous than most fintech postings admit. You will spend real time on idempotency keys, on ACH return codes, on why a ledger entry posted twice during a partial network failure at 2am. Our on-call rotation is one week in six, and the person who broke something is the person who writes the postmortem.

What we need from you:

1. Seven or more years writing backend services, at least two in a system where being wrong costs money.
2. Deep Postgres knowledge. Not ORM familiarity — you can read a query plan and know when a transaction isolation level is the actual bug.
3. Go, or the demonstrated ability to learn it in a month. Several of our strongest engineers arrived from Java and Python.
4. Comfort with ambiguity in requirements from our compliance and treasury teams, who know what they need but not always how to describe it in a ticket.

Nice to have: exposure to card networks, double-entry accounting systems, or SOC 2 audits.

Our process is four steps: a 45-minute call with the hiring manager, a take-home you can finish in three hours (we pay $400 for it), a system design conversation, and a half-day with the team. Two weeks start to finish. We tell you no quickly if the answer is no.

The text above has these problems. Rewrite it so none remain.
Change nothing else, and keep the same length and purpose.

- colon_reveal (Nice to have:):
- paragraph_uniformity (4 paragraphs, spread 0.31):

Return only the rewritten text.
